name: Chittagonian (Retired)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Retired ISO bookkeeping code (cit split into rhg/ctg in 2007); not a describable languoid.

new_statements.quote: (6) In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian and Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened; thus হওয়ালা (Arab. حواله) "charge" becomes হাওলা "a háola" (a tenure in which the tenant receives "charge" of a tract of jungle to be reclaimed); এলাকা (Arab. علاقة) "connexion" becomes এলকা.
new_statements.citation: Pargiter, F. E. 1886. Notes on the Chittagong Dialect. Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal 55, Part I, No. 1, pp. 66 ff. (repeated verbatim in Grierson 1903, Linguistic Survey of India V.1, p. 293)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (identical copy of, same size 230731 B). The page carries the running head "F. E. Pargiter—Notes on the Chittagong Dialect. [No. 1," and, under the "Corruption of Words" list, item (6) reads exactly: "In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian and Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened; thus হওয়ালা (Arab. حواله) "charge" becomes হাওলা "a háola" (a tenure in which the tenant receives "charge" of a tract of jungle to be reclaimed); এলাকা (Arab. علاقة) "connexion" becomes এলকা." The English matches the compiler quote word for word (the Bengali/Arabic glyphs are as legible as a 1886 scan allows). Page nu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In polysyllabic words the accent is retracted as far toward the beginning of the word as possible, i.e. onto the initial syllable, and the post-tonic syllables are reduced (vowel loss: haoyala > háola, elaka > élka). Stated most explicitly for Perso-Arabic loans.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rule is qualified 'especially those borrowed from Persian and Arabic'. Note the tension with Ray, Hai & Ray 1966 sec. 13.4 (p. 94), the only modern phonological description opened, which finds 'a system of lexically significant pitch shapes, or tones' with 'one and only one contrastive tone' per independent word (rising, falling, level) and gives no word-stress placement rule in sec. 13.5 'Intonation and accent'. For the Rohingya half of the retired code, Largin & Erden 2019 and Kuykendall 2025 (p. 45) report lexically contrastive stress/high pitch on 'a few words' (gor 'do' vs gór 'house'), analysis 'only preliminary', no placement rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of isolated words; Pargiter's is a 19th-century pre-phonemic note by a colonial administrator, not an instrumental or phonemic analysis. Confidence low.
new_statements.identity_note: chit1285 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping languoid, not a language: it is the retired ISO 639-3 code [cit] 'Chittagonian', split by change request 2006-048 (adopted 2007-07-18) into [ctg] Chittagonian = chit1275 and [rhg] Rohingya = rohi1238. Every source read describes one of those two: Pargiter 1886, Grierson 1903, Ray/Hai/Ray 1966 and Barua 2020 describe Chittagonian (chit1275, itself a separate WORLD_TARGET with these files already held); Largin & Erden 2019, Kuykendall 2025, RLF 2011 and the IOM dictionary describe Rohingya (rohi1238, already handled). by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) the quoted statement should be filed under chit1275, not chit1285.

sources.note: Front matter: 'There are still many open questions e.g. the stress/tone system which the three scripts have different approaches on'. No analysis.

sources.citation: Barua, Amit. 2020. A Comparative Study of Phonological Bengali Language and Chittagonian Dialect Spoken in Bangladesh. MA thesis (Linguistics), Mahachulalongkornrajavidyalaya University, 130 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Segmental comparison only (vowels, consonants). p. 14 generic definition of stress/pitch/intonation as suprasegmentals; p. 24 (on Bengali diphthongs) 'falling diphthongs with the stress on the first element, if there is any stress'; p. 98 lists 'syllable structure, stress.. and intonation' of Chittagonian as topics for future research. Mentions children not speaking Chittagonian 'with correct tones' (p. 8) without analysis.

sources.citation: Largin, J. & O. Erden. 2019. A brief grammar of Rohingya. learnrohingya.com (Internet Archive copy).
sources.note: sec. 'Vowels (oral, nasalized and stressed)': 'A few words in Rohingya receive stress on the vowel. Where there is a clear distinction in meaning, the acute accent can be added on the vowel that receives the stress, as in bai "through" vs. bái "brother" and gor- "do" vs. gór "house." Otherwise, context will determine the meaning of words that have stressed vowels.' Lexically contrastive; no placement rule; sketch for non-linguists, formal analysis promised.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Rohingya language' (phonology cites Rohingya Language Foundation 2011 and Largin & Erden 2019).
sources.note: 'Accented vowels, marked with an acute accent, represent stressed (or hard) vowels, and repeating a vowel lengthens it.. tonals are marked by arranging the location of a stressed vowel in a lengthened pair, like aá and áa.' Second-hand.

sources.citation: Ray, Punya Sloka, Muhammad Abdul Hai & Lila Ray. 1966. Bengali Language Handbook. Washington, D.C.: Center for Applied Linguistics. Ch. 13 'Chittagong dialect', pp. 89-97.
sources.note: sec. 13.4 Tones, p. 94: 'There is a system of lexically significant pitch shapes, or tones. An independent word.. has one and only one contrastive tone' (rising, falling, level; first tone dominates the phrase). sec. 13.5 Intonation and accent, pp. 94-95: 'Intonational stresses and lengths are strikingly different from those of the standard' -- pre-pausal syllable-final lengthening, stem/suffix syllable division, intonation contours; no statement of where word stress falls. Author warns the description rests on 'an inadequate sampling and an equally inadequate analysis' (p. 89).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. 1903. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. V Part I (Bengali & Assamese). South-Eastern Dialect (Chittagong District), p. 293.
sources.note: p. 293 repeats Pargiter verbatim: 'In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian or Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened.'

sources.citation: r12a.github.io, Hanifi Rohingya orthography notes (cites Wikipedia only); rohingyalanguage.org/learn/pronunciation (no author, no sources).
sources.note: r12a: 'Rohingya has 3 tones. They indicate stress and vowel length' (short-high, long-falling, long-rising). rohingyalanguage.org: 'The acute accents á é í ó ú do not change the vowel sound -- they mark stress: say the syllable harder and with a higher pitch' (ful bridge vs fúl flower). Both unsourced.

sources.note: p. 20: 'Vowel length is also assumed to be contrastive, as is stress, which appears to interact with vowel length (Largin and Erden 2019).
